title: Advancing equity in cross-cultural psychology: embracing diverse epistemologies and fostering collaborative practices
tldr: This review examines how colonial legacies and Western dominance marginalize Global South scholars in cross-cultural psychology and proposes pathways toward equitable collaboration.
problem_and_motivation: Cross-cultural psychology has been historically dominated by Western perspectives, methodologies, and interests, with over 95% of research samples drawn from WEIRD populations. This marginalization of Global South scholarship has roots in colonial practices including intellectual extractivism, leading to publication disparities and underrepresentation. The field lacks a comprehensive critical assessment of these inequities and actionable strategies for more inclusive research practices.
approach: Conducted a narrative literature review synthesizing insights from colonial theory, indigenous psychology, and cross-cultural research methodology.
Examined the Global North-South dichotomy as a heuristic for discussing systemic inequalities in knowledge production.
Analyzed the legacy of colonialism and its specific implications for psychological scholarship and intellectual extractivism.
Reviewed challenges of representation including translation issues, ethnocentrism, stereotype reinforcement, and intra-cultural diversity.
Explored the economics of knowledge production including funding disparities, access barriers, and authorship inequities.
Proposed actionable strategies for equitable collaboration based on lived experience and literature synthesis.
findings: num: Over 95% of psychology research samples from 2003-2018 drawn from WEIRD populations.
num: Non-WEIRD sample representation increased only from 3% to 4% over 15 years.
num: Mixed-methods survey of 232 researchers revealed biases against Majority World research.
num: Editorial board diversity directly correlates with diversity of published articles.
Non-White scientists face prolonged review periods and lower citation rates than White scientists.

Open access article processing charges create new financial barriers for underfunded institutions.

topics.name: User Trust in Personal Finance Systems
topics.justification: Discusses trust dynamics in academic knowledge systems and power asymmetries between institutions and marginalized communities.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: The paper provides a comprehensive critical review of colonial legacies and structural inequities in cross-cultural psychology. It synthesizes evidence on WEIRD sample dominance, intellectual extractivism, and publication disparities affecting Global South scholars. The review articulates the Global North-South dichotomy as a more nuanced framework than East-West or WEIRD-non-WEIRD comparisons for discussing knowledge production asymmetries. It proposes ten actionable strategies for equitable collaboration including tiered fee structures, local research leadership, and indigenous methodology integration. The paper contributes a framework for understanding how economic, historical, and geopolitical factors shape whose knowledge is produced and valued in psychological science.
directly_justifies: Over 95% of psychology research samples from 2003-2018 were drawn from WEIRD populations globally.
Intellectual extractivism involves extracting knowledge from communities without adequate recognition or compensation.
Non-White scientists face systemic inequalities in editorial representation and citation rates.
Global South scholars may tailor research to fit Northern funding interests, sacrificing local relevance.
Tiered fee structures for publication charges can mitigate financial barriers for Global South scholars.
limits: The paper is a narrative review rather than a systematic review, limiting reproducibility of its synthesis.
The Global North-South dichotomy, while acknowledged, may oversimplify diversity within these regions.
The paper does not provide empirical data to support all claims about publication disparities.
The scope is limited to cross-cultural psychology and does not address other social science disciplines.
No quantitative meta-analysis was conducted to measure the extent of representation gaps.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: All 14 topic domains were systematically scanned. No domain from the personal finance taxonomy directly corresponds to this paper's subject matter, as it is a review of equity and decolonization in cross-cultural psychology. Topic 10.B (User Trust in Personal Finance Systems) was selected as the only code with contextual relevance, since the paper discusses trust dynamics and power asymmetries in knowledge production, which shares structural parallels with trust concerns in user-facing systems. All other domains (financial demographics, expense categorization, predictive modeling, budgeting, anomaly detection, mobile design, data privacy, engagement, evaluation, savings/debt management, synthetic data, and ML deployment) were considered and rejected as they concern personal finance technology specifically, which this paper does not address. The paper is fundamentally a meta-scientific critique of academic practice rather than a contribution to any topic in the personal finance systems taxonomy.

limitations: The paper is a narrative review without systematic methodology, potentially limiting comprehensiveness and reproducibility.
The Global North-South dichotomy is acknowledged as reductive but still applied as the primary analytical framework.
No original empirical data is presented to quantify the extent of representation or citation disparities.
The scope is confined to cross-cultural psychology and does not generalize to other social science disciplines.
Practical implementation challenges of proposed strategies are not empirically evaluated.
remember_this: Over 95% of psychological research samples between 2003-2018 came from WEIRD populations.
Intellectual extractivism mirrors colonial resource extraction by taking knowledge without reciprocity.
Global South scholars face systemic barriers in editorial representation, citation rates, and funding access.
Tiered publication fees and local research leadership are proposed as concrete equity interventions.
The Global North-South dichotomy offers a more nuanced lens than East-West for analyzing knowledge asymmetries.
